title: Tuba
reference_instrument: University of Iowa MIS tuba (Mirafone 1865U CC tuba, performer D. Spies, per MIStuba.html)
summary: Limits: a bore read off a raster figure (within 5 mm along the tube and 1.5 mm in diameter, 10 % at the leadpipe) of a tuba of unnamed make; a mouthpiece whose cup diameter and throat are a printed tuba mouthpiece's (Denis Wick 3 and 3L, 31.25 mm and 8.78 mm) laid over a tenor trombone's profile, with its cup depth and backbore still the trombone's; valve loops of the card's own arithmetic; lip and blowing borrowed from a trombone; the recordings are Iowa's Mirafone CC tuba, a different instrument; every note is darker than its recording and too clean. The bore is the profile in Fig. 3 of Campbell and Myers (2023, CC BY 3.0). Bb2, B2 and G3 sound on it from a lip ladder, with no pitch an input, each also rendered without the mouthpiece; C2 stays empty, since its loop sounds 146 c sharp and no setting holds it. The family is graded from the second harmonic upward.
physics_present: the bore: one tuba's profile read off Fig. 3 of Campbell and Myers (2023, open access under CC BY 3.0), 3.627 m, 54 cones from x = 20 mm to a bell rim of 273.6 mm, within 5 mm along the tube and 1.5 mm in diameter; the engine's own scan puts its resonances on an F tuba's series from the second to the tenth within 80 c, and nothing was fitted to get that

a mouthpiece whose cup diameter and throat are a printed tuba mouthpiece's, laid over the tenor-trombone mouthpiece of the trombone card (Braden 2006, Fig. 5.3, digitised from a figure): the printed Denis Wick Classic tuba 3 and 3L, cup diameter 31.25 mm and bore (throat) 8.78 mm, read three times (the maker's published data as tabulated by Mouthpiece Express, and the Thomann and Weiner Music listings), against a spread of printed tuba cups of 29.5 to 33.27 mm with throats of 7.62 to 8.78 mm, 31.25 mm being also the median of the nine printed Bach tuba cups; the first 13 cones (rim to throat) and the next 6 (backbore) are mapped affinely in radius over the trombone's, the rim from 12.860 to 15.625 mm, the throat from 3.885 to 4.390 mm and the backbore's exit kept at 5.163 mm, with every length unchanged, so the cup volume rises 1.45 times, from 10.0 to 14.5 cm3; the cup depth and the backbore's length and exit radius are still the trombone's, the tuba the bore was read from is of unnamed make so its own mouthpiece is not known, and the flow-noise row's duct radius is the printed cup's rim radius, 15.625 mm, in place of the trombone cup's 12.86 mm

valve loops of the card's own arithmetic: the bore's 3.627 m times 2^(n/12) - 1 of straight tube (215.7 mm for B2, 444.2 mm for Bb2 and G3), n the open bore's nearest resonance above the note rounded, spliced at the 16.4 mm station nearest 1 m from the mouthpiece; derived, not measured, no bends or ports

the horn card's lip, blowing and microphone, which are the tenor trombone's: Cullen's (2000) embouchure 19, a flat 6.22 kPa from rest, a flanged modal bell, the receiver 1.524 m on axis with a declared 3.9 kHz band, and the flow-noise row at the lips (Oldham and Ukpoho 1990, extrapolated)

the lip's flow-area exponent as a trombonist's lips measured it, per note: Bromage, Campbell and Gilbert (2010, preprint HAL hal-00474644v1, Table 2; one trombonist, AJ, mezzo forte, high-speed video; 1.2 at Bb1, 1.3 at Bb2, 1.6 at F3, 1.9 at F4): q = 1.300 on Bb2 (the table's own value), 1.343 on B2 and 1.650 on G3 (linear interpolation in MIDI between the printed notes, no extrapolation), in place of the 1.4 borrowed from a trombone; a trombonist's lips, not a tuba player's; the count moved from 6 to 6 of 14 on Bb2, 5 to 5 of 14 on B2 and 5 to 7 of 15 on G3

notes from a lip ladder: seven lip settings per note, and the lowest one that holds a single partial for its last second within 60 c of the note is the page's; no pitch is an input and the lip multiplier is a player's setting that no print gives
physics_missing: A tuba mouthpiece's cup depth and backbore profile, and the tuba player's own mouthpiece: makers' catalogues print a cup diameter and a throat but give the depth and the backbore only as words (deep, large barrel), and Myers 1998 prints tuba cup volumes and shank diameters only, so no depth in millimetres and no backbore profile is printed in the open sources found. The cup depth and the backbore on the three pages are the tenor trombone's (Braden 2006, Fig. 5.3), under a printed tuba cup diameter and throat (Denis Wick 3 and 3L, 31.25 and 8.78 mm); the tuba the bore was read from is of unnamed make, so its player's mouthpiece is not known. The borrowed trombone mouthpiece moved the notes (Bb2 36 c, B2 34 c and G3 22 c lower at the same lip setting); the printed cup diameter and throat moved the held notes a further 14.2 c (Bb2), 13.6 c (B2) and 9.9 c (G3) lower, the level by under 0.4 dB, and the grader's count from 6 to 5 of 14 on B2, from 6 to 5 of 15 on G3 and from 5 to 6 of 14 on Bb2, so a tuba player's mouthpiece would move them again

The specimen: the paper does not name the tuba, and its length is F-length, while the recordings are Iowa's Mirafone 1865U CC tuba, so a note's pitch agreeing with a recording is a coincidence, not a check; the printed bell rims of the Mirafone 186 model are 415.9 mm (a 1966 186-5U in the Simonetti collection) and 450 mm (current dealer listings) against this bore's 273.6 mm, with a printed valve-section bore of 19.6 mm and printed heights of 960 mm (the CC) and 1016 mm (the BBb), and no tubing, leadpipe or bell profile of it is printed in anything found (searched 2026-11-09: dealer and collection pages, Myers 1998, Table 1 of the ghost-note paper of Matteoli and colleagues, six video demonstrations in which no frame shows the bell edge-on with a scale), so the bore stays a declared stand-in; a bore rebuilt from a rim, a valve bore and a pitch would be invented, not printed

Valves: only the loops of the notes shown exist, as straight tube spliced in the narrow leadpipe, which makes the bore's resonances sit above the length arithmetic and more so as the loop grows; every other valve combination, the fourth valve and the tuning slide are absent

C2: the four-semitone loop puts the bore's second resonance 146 c above C2, and none of seventeen lip settings holds a note within 60 c of it (the closest is 148 c sharp). The rule was fixed before the render and no second loop was tried

The sound: H2 to H5 are 3 to 26 dB under the recordings, with dips made at the lip, the spectral centroid is 0.56 to 0.72 of the recordings', the floor between the harmonics below 1 kHz is 12 to 38 dB too clean, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio is 5 to 14 dB too high

A tuba player's lip: the lip is an artificial latex lip measured on a trombone-size mouthpiece, with channel width and rest gap that are not a tuba player's; no tuba player's lip is measured in anything printed that was found (Matteoli and colleagues, 2022, write that in vivo measurements of lip parameters would be very valuable), and no tuba blowing pressure is printed, only a model threshold above 3 kPa for the C contrabass tuba's pedal note

The chamber cutoff of the Iowa recording room below which the tuba's fundamentals are not trustworthy (the pages state absorption down to 60 Hz): the family is graded from the second harmonic upward until it is sourced, as the bead states

A player's tract upstream of the lip (opt-in, fs-couple brass_loop): the digitized LOW tract of one trumpeter (Kaburagi, Yamada, Fukui and Minamiya 2011, Fig. 3, Eb4, 311 Hz; section 0 removed, with the yielding wall of the voice cards) was tried as a declared stand-in on Bb2 (116.54 Hz), B2 (123.47 Hz) and G3 (196.0 Hz), the measured pitch lying 194.5, 187.5 and 115 Hz above them, a trumpeter's tract on a tuba. All three renders were refused by the airway at the pages' 9600 Hz before any sound (the converged characteristic line violates 4x-oversampled passivity), while the same tract and wall passed at 48000 Hz on the trumpet Bb3 page. No tuba player's tract was found, no tract value was adjusted, and the three tuba pages keep their cards; the three cards are to be re-run unchanged when the airway's rung climb for this refusal lands.
